conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martin, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the emotional support you deserve after having your baby.  
Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—better known as the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else. We’ll just talk through each question together; it usually takes only a few minutes.

Let’s start with the first question:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, most of the time it feels pretty difficult. I still laugh if my husband or sister makes a joke, but it’s like the sound comes out of habit—I don’t feel that light, happy lift I used to get. Things that used to crack me up just seem kind of “meh” now, like the joy is muted or behind a fog.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I feel like I’m stuck on the second-to-last answer—I’ve laughed a couple of times, but I really had to force it, and it didn’t feel like it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I picked the second-to-last one again. I still get a little spark of excitement when I think about meeting a friend for coffee or taking the baby for a walk, but it’s way smaller than before—like someone turned the volume down. Most things feel like chores I “should” do rather than stuff I truly look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I ended up circling the second-to-last box again. If the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” Even little stuff—like forgetting to bring a burp cloth—makes me feel like I’ve failed him somehow. I know, rationally, that babies just spit up and cry, but the guilty voice in my head still pipes up most days.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I marked the second-to-last one. Pretty much every day I catch myself running through “what-ifs” about the baby—like what if he stops breathing in the bassinet, or what if I trip on the stairs while I’m holding him. There’s no real reason for it; he’s healthy and the monitor’s fine. But the worries just pop up and loop until I check on him one more time.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I circled the second-to-last one again. It’s happened several times this week—out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath, even when nothing’s actually wrong. I’ll be folding laundry or warming a bottle and suddenly feel this wave of dread, like something bad is about to happen, even though everything’s quiet.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… I shaded in the second-to-last box. Most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I manage to feed and change him, wash the bottles, maybe grab a shower, but it’s like every small task piles up and I’m constantly behind. When he starts crying right as I sit down to eat, it feels like the universe is piling on. I don’t fall apart, but I do end up standing in the kitchen with tears in my eyes more often than I’d like to admit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I picked the second-to-last one. I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t turn off—keeps replaying everything I might have messed up or imagined dangers to the baby. It takes me a long time to drift off, and then I jolt awake at least once or twice with my heart pounding and those same worries spinning.
I have felt sad or miserable

I shaded the second-to-last box. I feel sad or empty most of the day—like there’s a heavy blanket on me—but it lifts a little when someone visits or when the baby gives me a sleepy grin. It’s not every single second, but it’s definitely more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I circled the second-to-last one. It’s happened a couple of times this week—usually when I’m alone with the baby and everything feels like too much. I’ll just start crying while I’m feeding him or trying to soothe him, but I can stop after a few minutes. It’s not an all-day thing, but it’s definitely more than I used to cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I… I shaded the second box. It’s crossed my mind once or twice, like a quick, scary flash—what if I just wasn’t here anymore—but I haven’t made any plans and I don’t want to act on it. I’m mostly scared that I even have the thought, and I’d never want to leave my baby.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Screening Note – Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) responses reviewed 7–10 days postpartum.

Symptom profile  
Predominant mood: persistent low/“empty,” with brief partial lifts during positive infant cues.  
Anhedonia: marked reduction in pleasure and anticipatory enjoyment (described as “volume turned down”).  
Guilt/worthlessness: automatic self-blame for routine infant care issues.  
Anxiety: daily pervasive worry, nocturnal rumination, episodic panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, dread).  
Functional impact: difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep, feeling “treading water,” tearful episodes when alone.  
Safety: Passive suicidal cognition twice (“what if I just wasn’t here”) without intent or plan; patient expresses fear of the thought and strong protective feelings toward infant.

Pattern  
Consistent endorsement of second-to-last response option across nine items (suggesting moderate-severe symptom intensity on traditional 0–3 scoring). No contradictory or minimising responses noted.

Screening significance  
Findings exceed threshold for probable major depressive episode with anxious features; marked distress and impaired coping; passive suicidal ideation present → elevated risk requiring immediate safety assessment and follow-up.

Risk factors documented  
– Postpartum hormonal/psychosocial stressors  
– Primiparous status  
– Sleep deprivation secondary to mood rather than infant demands alone  
– Absence of reported support during crying episodes

Next step (per protocol)  
Urgent referral for comprehensive clinical evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options; consider expedited mental health appointment within 24–48 h.
